artifacts.notes:
Two hundred and seventeen rows. Each names both arrangements it speaks about, so no
column means anything by its position; the psalm concordance beside this one does not,
and its hebrew column in fact records the Vulgate's division of a psalm under Hebrew
numbers, which is a third thing named for neither.

Six relations are expressible: one-to-one, split-right, merged-right, absent-right,
absent-left and not-recorded. The psalm concordance can say only the first, because its
schema requires both runs of a row to be the same length. Three of the six are needed in
Esther 15 alone. The Vulgate's 15:1-3, Mardochai's charge repeated from 4:8, is absent
from the Greek. Its 15:13 "thou shalt not die" and 15:14 "come near then, and touch the
sceptre" are the Greek's single 15:10. Its 15:15, which holds the sceptre, the embrace
and "why dost thou not speak to me", is the Greek's 15:11 and 15:12. Daniel needs the
same: the Vulgate's 3:52 carries both "blessed art thou, O Lord, the God of our fathers"
and "blessed is the holy name of thy glory", which the Greek numbers 29 and 30, and that
one merge is the whole of the difference between the Canticle's sixty-eight Greek verses
and the Vulgate's sixty-seven.

What was established, and against what.

Esther. Chapters 1 to 10:3 agree verse for verse. The Vulgate's 10:4-16:24 is the Greek
additions, which the Revised Version and the King James print as a separate book under
the Vulgate's own numbers -- except in chapter 15, where they do not: the Greek's 15:1
is the Vulgate's 15:4, and the chapter also holds the merge and the split described
above. The claim that that book carries the Vulgate's numbers throughout is therefore
wrong, and this table follows the text.

Daniel. Chapters 1 to 3:23 agree. The Vulgate's 3:24-90 is the Song of the Three, and
the correspondence is not an offset: after the merge at 3:52 the two traditions order
the Benedicite differently from 3:53 to 3:78 and realign at 3:79. The throne and the
depths are exchanged, the angels and the heavens are exchanged, the fountains and the
seas are exchanged, and the Vulgate keeps its four couplets of cold together where the
Greek sets nights and days and light and darkness between them. Every one of those
twenty-six correspondences was read. The Vulgate's 3:91-97 is the Greek's 3:24-30, its
3:98-100 is the Greek's 4:1-3, and its chapter 4 therefore runs three verses behind.
Susanna is Daniel 13:1-64. Daniel 13:65, "and king Astyages was gathered to his
fathers", is Bel 1, so Bel runs one verse ahead of Vulgate Daniel 14 from beginning to
end, and Vulgate 14:42 has no counterpart at all. The assertion in guidance/versification
section 7.2 that Susanna and Bel are pure chapter relabelling, verse for verse, is wrong
on both counts.

Ecclesiasticus. Recorded as not-recorded, which is a finding and not a gap. Measured
against the tracked texts, the Vulgate and the Greek differ in all fifty-one chapters,
not in the seven that had been reported; only 412 of the Douay's 1591 verses stand at
the same number in the World English Catholic Edition's 1359; six chapters share no
number at all; and the dominant mechanism is the Latin subdividing a Greek bicolon,
which happens some two hundred and thirty times. An alignment can be computed between
the two English translations, but they are translations of different languages and the
computation is a candidate, not a reading. One locus is recorded, because it was settled
by reading the verse: the introit Da pacem Domine sustinentibus te is the Vulgate's
36:18 and the Greek's 36:16, and the Greek's own 36:18 is the proverb of the belly.

What is deliberately not modelled.

The Catholic Public Domain Version's Esther. It prints the book in the Septuagint's
narrative order and in fifteen chapters of its own division: its 1:1 is the Vulgate's
11:2, its 2:1 is the Vulgate's 12:1, its 3:1 is the Vulgate's 1:1, and its chapter 5
holds thirteen verses where the Vulgate's chapter 3 holds fifteen. The chapter
boundaries fall inside Vulgate chapters, so this is a re-chaptering of the book and not
a renumbering of it; one edition witnesses it and no calendar cites it. Its Esther stays
refused wholesale by the rows that edition's own verse-alias artifact already carries.

The Brenton Septuagint, for the same reason and by the same earlier decision.

A verse-level Ecclesiasticus concordance, as above.

Two divergences found while compiling this and left for their owners. The tracked
Clementine Vulgate divides Ecclesiasticus 29:16 into three verses where the Douay has
two, and runs one ahead of it to the end of that chapter, so the Latin witnesses
disagree with each other there; it is not recorded here because this table is between
arrangements and that is a departure between two witnesses of one. And the King James
Apocrypha repeats the mountains of Song of the Three 53 at its verse 55, where the
Revised Version and the Latin both have the seas and rivers, so its 55 and 56 are one
line out of step; that is a textual defect rather than a numbering one and is declared,
with both openings and checked against both texts, in scripts/_deuterocanon.py.

artifacts.notes: 8661 rows across 1332 non-psalm chapters: 2239 concurring, at which a break is set, and 6422 disputed, at which none is. So the witnesses concur at 2239 of the 8661 positions where either of them breaks — 25.9 per cent. That figure is the measured disagreement between two modern English typesettings of the same books, and it is the reason the rule requires concurrence instead of taking a majority or a first witness: paragraph division in these editions is an editorial act, the editors disagree about it three times in four, and a break asserted on one witness alone would read as this edition's own. Beyond these positions, 21752 verses are broken by neither witness, 1679 are carried by neither, and 2380 stand in the excluded Psalms. Two witnesses were considered and refused. eBible.org's eng-rv is not used: its transcription of the Revised Version records 386 prose paragraph openings across 80 books — one of them mid-chapter in the whole protocanon — so it does not carry the Revised Version's paragraphing at all, and under a rule requiring every carrying witness to concur it would have vetoed almost every break rather than testifying about any. That is a fact about the file, not about the Revised Version, which was the first major English Bible set in true paragraphs. eBible.org's engDRA and latVUC are not used because they have nothing to say: their paragraph-opening sets are identical to each other and consist of one marker per non-psalm chapter. Two better witnesses exist and are NOT used here, both requiring entry to the source library under guidance/sources.md, which is a human-review gate and not a derivation. First, eBible.org's engkjvcpb is F. H. A. Scrivener's Cambridge Paragraph Bible of 1873, public domain, and the only English witness whose editor documented his method — he states it in The Authorized Edition of the English Bible (1611) (Cambridge, 1884, pp. 128-129), aiming between breaks 'too far apart for the reader's convenience' and 'a virtual return to the discarded verse divisions', and reports a remarkable resemblance between his paragraphs and the 1871 Church Lectionary lesson boundaries. It carries 1987 mid-chapter prose openings in the protocanon. Adding it would make the rule a real two-of-three rather than a unanimity of two. Second, and older than any of them, the Masoretic petuchah and setumah section divisions: verse-aligned, attested from the Dead Sea Scrolls, codified by Maimonides from the Aleppo Codex, and machine-readable under open terms in two independent encodings that agree — tanach.us UXLC ('All biblical Hebrew text, in any format, may be viewed or copied without restriction') and OpenScriptures morphhb (CC BY 4.0). They number 3162 across the 39 books of the Hebrew canon, a mean of 7.3 verses to a section, which is paragraph-scale in the narrative and prophetic books; they are far too coarse in the wisdom books and absent from the Psalms, and they do not reach the deuterocanon or the New Testament at all. They would be the oldest and best-attested witness available and should be the next thing acquired.
artifacts.rights_basis: This table carries no scripture text: it is a list of verse numbers at which a paragraph opens or is refused, derived from two public-domain witnesses that record paragraph structure of their own — eBible.org's eng-kjv and its public-domain World English Bible — and expressed in the Douay-Rheims numbering this repository cites in. The Douay and Rheims translation was published in 1582, 1609 and 1610 and Challoner revised it in 1749-1752, all long in the public domain. eBible.org asserts no separate claim over paragraph structure in any of its releases; its notices cover each work undifferentiated, and the World English Bible's single condition is triggered by changing the text, which this table does not do because it contains none. No authority was found holding that paragraph division in a public-domain text is itself copyrightable, and the general law runs the other way: under Feist v. Rural Telephone (499 U.S. 340, 1991) a compilation of public-domain material is protectable only where selection or arrangement shows minimal creativity, and an arrangement derived by a stated rule from witnesses is the paradigm of the mechanical case. The rows are a derivation this project performed and publishes as project-created content under CC BY 4.0, regenerable by anyone holding the two witness tables and this edition's own verse-alias table.

artifacts.notes: Triptych-compiled concordance between the Vulgate/Septuagint psalm numbering used throughout this edition and in the 1962 Missal, the Hebrew/Masoretic numbering used by the Nova Vulgata and by the New American Bible, and the English convention of the King James, Revised Standard, and most other modern English versions, which leaves the psalm inscription unnumbered. Rows are verse ranges, so the four places where one system joins or divides what the other keeps whole are exact. english_offset is the number of leading Vulgate verses occupied by the inscription; english_offset_uniform is "no" for the sixteen psalms where the two systems also divide the body differently, so that the offset holds only from the head of the psalm. The chapter correspondences and the four split points were checked against the Clementine Latin and against the printed 1914 John Murphy edition; the offsets were computed from the extracted verse counts against a King James Version consulted online and not retained, and every psalm inscription was read. Correction of 2026-07-31. Hebrew 13 was flagged uniform and is not. Computing the offsets from verse counts could not catch it: the Douay's Psalm 12 and the English Psalm 13 both print six verses, and the divergences cancel. The Douay's verse 1 carries the inscription together with the first line of the poem, so it takes no verse of its own and english_offset is rightly 0; but the Douay then divides "How long shall I take counsels in my soul" from "How long shall my enemy be exalted over Me?" into verses 2 and 3 where the King James and the Revised Version hold both in verse 2, and it keeps in its verse 6 what they divide between 5 and 6. Vulgate 12:4 is English 13:3. The row now reads english_offset_uniform "no" and the psalm is refused rather than shifted. The correction was made against the tracked Clementine, Douay-Rheims, King James and Revised Version 1895 chapter files, not against the counts.

work.description: The English Catholic Bible translated from the Latin Vulgate by the English College in exile: the New Testament published at Rheims in 1582 and the Old Testament at Douay in 1609 and 1610, revised by Bishop Richard Challoner between 1749 and 1752. It is the English counterpart of the Clementine Vulgate the 1962 Missal prints. Edition records must keep the original Douay and Rheims text, Challoner's revision, the 1899 and 1914 American printings, and later electronic transcriptions apart, because their wording and in places their versification differ. A locus is BookToken.chapter.verse, optionally with a closing verse or chapter.verse after a hyphen, as in Ps.53.6-7, 1Cor.10.6-13, or Dan.3.49-51. The 73 book tokens, the modern names and 1962 Missal abbreviations they answer to, and the naming traps are registered in the book index of each electronic edition. Chapter and verse numbers are always the Vulgate ones the Missal cites, never modern Hebrew ones: Psalm numbers follow the Septuagint and Vulgate series, so Ps 53 here is Ps 54 in a modern Bible, and Douay 1 and 2 Kings are modern 1 and 2 Samuel. The psalm-numbering and verse-alias tables registered with the text carry the exhaustive conversions.
